title: Comparing, and the fourth case
goal: Compare two things and name the "most" — while meeting the last case, eignarfall, which handles possession and a few important prepositions.
bekal: use *en* for "than" and recognize five irregular comparisons
form eignarfall for possession and after *til*, *vegna*, *án*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Veðrið og nafnið
dialogs.intro: Early January, and a north wind is blowing. A chat about the weather leads to a thousand-year-old lie.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Í dag er kaldara en í gær.
lines.literal: in day is colder than in yesterday.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Já, og á morgun verður enn kaldara.
lines.id: Yes, and tomorrow will be even colder.
lines.literal: yes, and on morrow becomes still colder.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.id: Is the winter always this long?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Hann er lengri en á Spáni, en styttri en í Síberíu.
lines.id: It's longer than in Spain, but shorter than in Siberia.
lines.literal: it is longer than in Spain, but shorter than in Siberia.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Það er lítil huggun! Hver er kaldasti mánuðurinn?
lines.id: That's small comfort! Which month is the coldest?
lines.literal: that is small comfort! which is coldest month-the?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Janúar. En veðrið í Reykjavík er mildara en margir halda.
lines.id: January. But the weather in Reykjavík is milder than many people think.
lines.literal: January. but weather-the in Reykjavík is milder than many think.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Vegna Golfstraumsins. Hitastig sjávarins bjargar okkur.
lines.id: Because of the Gulf Stream. The sea temperature saves us.
lines.literal: because-of Gulf-Stream-the. temperature sea-the's saves us.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.id: So the country's name is misleading?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Algjörlega. Grænland er ísi lagt, og Ísland er grænt.
lines.id: Completely. Greenland is covered in ice, and Iceland is green.
lines.literal: completely. Green-land is ice-laid, and Ice-land is green.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.id: Who gave the country that name?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Víkingur sem var í vondu skapi. Sagan er lengri en það, auðvitað.
lines.id: A Viking in a bad mood. The story is longer than that, of course.
lines.literal: Viking who was in bad mood. story-the is longer than that, of-course.

notes: **En means two things: "but" and "than".** *Hann er lengri **en** á Spáni* (than), but *lengri **en** styttri* (but). What decides is whether a comparative comes before it. English uses two different words, so this takes a little getting used to.

**Comparatives are formed with -ari or -ri**: *kaldur → kaldari*, *langur → lengri*, *mildur → mildari*. The *most* form takes **-astur** or **-stur**: *kaldastur*, *lengstur* — like English *-er* and *-est*.
**Hvers vegna is literally "of what way".** *Hvers* is the eignarfall form of *hver*. The phrase is frozen — used as it is and freely swapped with *af hverju*, which you've known since unit 10.

**Vegna and til are always followed by eignarfall (genitive)**: *vegna Golfstraums**ins***, *til Reykjavík**ur***, *nafn lands**ins***. This is the fourth and last case — the least used, which is why it comes last.

**Nafn landsins — how Icelandic expresses possession.** The pattern: the thing first, then the owner in eignarfall. *Bíll Önnu* (Anna's car), *hús Jóns* (Jón's house). The order is like English "the car of Anna" — but the ending works like English *'s*.

**The two countries' names really are swapped, and on purpose.** According to *Landnámabók*, Eiríkur rauði (Erik the Red) named the ice island "Green Land" so people would want to move there with him. Iceland, meanwhile, was named "Ice Land" by one of its first settlers after seeing pack ice in a fjord — and according to the saga, he was in a very bad mood.

grammars.title: -er and -est
body: Two endings to learn, and five irregular words — which happen to be the ones you'll use most.
after: The five words in bold are irregular — just as irregular as English *good–better–best*, because they come from the same roots. If you know the English pattern, you practically know this one already.
The *most* form usually takes an article: *kaldast**i** mánuðurinn* (the coldest month), *best**a** bókin* (the best book). The endings **-i** and **-a** are the marker.
To say "as … as": *jafn … og* — *Ísland er jafn stórt og Jáva.* For "not as … as": *ekki eins … og*.

grammars.title: Eignarfall — the fourth case
body: The rarest case, but you can't avoid it: it handles possession and three very common prepositions.
after: The marker is easiest to spot in karlkyn and hvorugkyn: the ending **-s**, and **-sins** with the article. Kvenkyn takes **-u** or **-ar**, with the article **-nnar**.
Three prepositions that require it: **til** (to, until), **vegna** (because of), **án** (without). *Til Reykjavíkur*, *vegna veðursins*, *án hjálpar*.
Place names follow too: *til Ísland**s***, *til Akureyr**ar***, *til Reykjavík**ur***. If you've ever seen a road sign in Iceland, you've seen eignarfall dozens of times without knowing its name.

blocks.title: Wind, not cold
items: Reykjavík's average January temperature is around **zero degrees** — warmer than Oslo, Helsinki, or Moscow, and much warmer than people expect. What makes Iceland feel cold isn't the number but **the wind**.
That's why Icelanders rarely ask how many degrees it is; they ask *er hvasst?* — is it windy? And they complain about it every day, all year round, without ever getting tired of it.

blocks.text: *Til hamingju* is literally "to happiness" — and *hamingju* is the eignarfall of *hamingja*. The congratulations you've heard since the start turn out to be one more grammar lesson you'd quietly mastered already.

exercises.prompt: Write the *-er* and *-est* forms of these adjectives.

items: Í dag er ____ (kaldur) en í gær.
Þetta er ____ (góður) bókin sem ég hef lesið.
The weather is worse than yesterday.
Because of the weather, we're not going.
